$$0 = \frac{M}{2}v_1 - \frac{M}{2}v_2 \implies v_1 = v_2 \quad \dots(1)$$
From conservation of energy:
$$\Delta m c^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{M}{2}\right)v_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{M}{2}\right)v_2^2 \quad \dots(2)$$

question_text: A radioactive nucleus (initial mass number $A$ and atomic number $Z$) emits $3\alpha$-particles and $2$ positrons. The ratio of number of neutrons to that of protons in the final nucleus will be
solution:
In positive beta decay a proton is transformed into a neutron and a positron is emitted:
$$p^+ \rightarrow n^0 + e^+$$
No. of neutrons initially was $A - Z$.
No. of neutrons after decay:
$$N = (A - Z) - 3 \times 2 \text{ (due to } \alpha\text{-particles)} + 2 \times 1 \text{ (due to positive beta decay)} = A - Z - 6 + 2 = A - Z - 4$$
The number of protons will reduce by $8$ [as $3 \times 2$ (due to $\alpha$-particles) $+ 2$ (due to positive beta decay)]. Hence atomic number reduces to:
$$Z' = Z - 8$$
Therefore, the ratio of number of neutrons to protons is:
$$\frac{N}{Z'} = \frac{A - Z - 4}{Z - 8}$$

$N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t_2} \quad \lambda t_1 = \ln 3$

question_text: The counting rate observed from a radioactive source at $t = 0$ was $1600\text{ counts s}^{-1}$, and $t = 8\text{ s}$, it was $100\text{ counts s}^{-1}$. The counting rate observed as counts $\text{s}^{-1}$ at $t = 6\text{ s}$ will be
solution:
As we know,
$$\left[\frac{N}{N_0}\right] = \left[\frac{1}{2}\right]^n$$
$n =$ no. of half life
$N -$ no. of atoms left
$N_0 -$ initial no. of atoms

By radioactive decay law,
$$\frac{dN}{dt} = kN$$
$k -$ disintegration constant
$$\therefore \frac{\frac{dN}{dt}}{\frac{dN_0}{dt}} = \frac{N}{N_0}$$
From (i) and (ii) we get
$$\frac{\frac{dN}{dt}}{\frac{dN_0}{dt}} = \left[\frac{1}{2}\right]^n$$
or, $\left[\frac{100}{1600}\right] = \left[\frac{1}{2}\right]^n \Rightarrow \left[\frac{1}{2}\right]^4 = \left[\frac{1}{2}\right]^n$
$\therefore n = 4$, Therefore, in $8\text{ seconds}$ $4$ half life had occurred in which counting rate reduces to $100\text{ counts s}^{-1}$.
$\therefore\text{ Half life, } \frac{T_1}{2} = 2\text{sec}$
In $6\text{sec}$, $3$ half life will occur
$$\therefore \left[\frac{\frac{dN}{dt}}{1600}\right] = \left[\frac{1}{2}\right]^3$$
$$\Rightarrow \frac{dN}{dt} = 200\text{ counts s}^{-1}$$

question_text: A radioactive nuclei with decay constant $0.5/\text{s}$ is being produced at a constant rate of $100\text{ nuclei/s}$. If at $t = 0$ there were no nuclei, the time when there are $50$ nuclei is:
solution:
Let $N$ be the number of nuclei at any time $t$ then,
$$\frac{dN}{dt} = 100 - \lambda N$$
or
$$\int_0^N \frac{dN}{(100 - \lambda N)} = \int_0^t dt$$
$$-\frac{1}{\lambda} [\log(100 - \lambda N)]_0^N = t$$
$$\log(100 - \lambda N) - \log 100 = -\lambda t$$
$$\log\left(\frac{100 - \lambda N}{100}\right) = -\lambda t$$
$$\frac{100 - \lambda N}{100} = e^{-\lambda t}$$
$$1 - \frac{\lambda N}{100} = e^{-\lambda t}$$
$$N = \frac{100}{\lambda}(1 - e^{-\lambda t})$$
As, $N = 50$ and $\lambda = 0.5/\text{sec}$
$$\therefore 50 = \frac{100}{0.5}(1 - e^{-0.5t})$$
Solving we get,
$$t = 2\ln\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)\text{ sec}$$

[This question was awarded a bonus and proper correction was made to avoid that]
solution:
We know that,
The rate of decay at the time $t$ is
$$A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$$
$$2 = 20 \cdot e^{-\lambda t}$$

question_text: Let $N_\beta$ be the number of $\beta$ particle emitted by $1\text{ gram}$ of $\text{Na}^{24}$ radioactive nuclei having a half life of $15\text{ h}$. In $7.5\text{ h}$, the number $N_\beta$ is close to [$N_A = 6.023 \times 10^{23}\text{ mole}^{-1}$]
solution:
$\because \frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$
$N = \text{no. of un-decayed nuclei}$
$N_0 = \text{initial no. of nuclei}$
Also $t = n \times T_{\frac{1}{2}}$
$$\Rightarrow \frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{t}{T_{1/2}}}$$

$$\because N_0 = \frac{1}{24} \times 6.023 \times 10^{23}$$
$$\Rightarrow \text{No. of nuclei decayed} = 0.29 \times \frac{1}{24} \times 6.023 \times 10^{23}$$
$$= 0.0727 \times 10^{23}$$

question_text:

question_text: A solution containing active cobalt $Co2760$ having an activity of $0.8\mu\text{Ci}$ and decay constant $\lambda$ is injected in an animal's body. $\Rightarrow V = X \left(\frac{A_0}{A^1}\right) e^{-\lambda t} \Rightarrow V = (1\text{ cm}^3) \left(\frac{8 \times 10^{-7} \times 3.7 \times 10^{10}}{\frac{300}{60}}\right) (0.84)$

$= 4.97 \times 10^3\text{ cm}^3 = 4.97\text{ liter} \simeq 5\text{ L}$.

question_text: An unstable heavy nucleus at rest breaks into two nuclei which move away with velocities in the ratio of $8 : 27$. The ratio of the radii of the nuclei (assumed to be spherical) is :

According to question, $\frac{V_1}{V_2} = \frac{8}{27}$

$m_1 V_1 = m_2 V_2$ (Law of momentum conservation)

$\Rightarrow \frac{m_1}{m_2} = \frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{27}{8}$

$\frac{\rho \times \frac{4}{3}\pi R_1^3}{\rho \times \frac{4}{3}\pi R_2^3} = \frac{27}{8} \quad \left(\because \text{density } \rho = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\right)$

$\Rightarrow \left(\frac{R_1}{R_2}\right) = \left(\frac{27}{8}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} = \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{3 \times \frac{1}{3}}$

$\therefore \frac{R_1}{R_2} = \frac{3}{2}$

question_text: At a given instant, say $t = 0$, two radioactive substance $A$ and $B$ have equal activities. The ratio $\frac{R_B}{R_A}$ of their activities after time $t$ itself decays with time $t$ as $e^{-3t}$. If the half-life of $A$ is $\ln 2$, the half-life of $B$ is:
solution:
Given,
Half life of $A = \ln 2$

Initial number of nucleus is, $R_{0A} = R_{0B} = R_0$

Half life is related with decay constant as, $(t_{1/2})_A = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$

$\lambda_A = 1$

At $t = 0$, $R_A = R_B$

From activity relation, we have,
$R_0 e^{-\lambda_A T} = R_0 e^{-\lambda_B T}$

$\text{at } T = t, \Rightarrow \frac{R_B}{R_A} = \frac{R_0 e^{-\lambda_B t}}{R_0 e^{-\lambda_A t}}$

As per given question, $\frac{R_B}{R_A} = e^{-3t}$, On comparing with above relation, we have

$\Rightarrow e^{-(\lambda_B - \lambda_A)t} = e^{-3t}$

$\Rightarrow \lambda_B - \lambda_A = 3$

$\Rightarrow \lambda_B = 3 + 1 = 4$

$\Rightarrow (t_{1/2})_B = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda_B} = \frac{\ln 2}{4}$

question_text: A radioactive nucleus decays by two different processes. The half-life for the first process is $10\text{ s}$ and that for the second is $100\text{ s}$. The effective half-life of the nucleus is close to:
solution:
Using the equation of radioactive decay law, $-\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda_1 N + \lambda_2 N \dots(1)$

$-\frac{dN}{dt} = (\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)N \dots(2)$ Where, $-\frac{dN}{dt}$ is the rate of decay, $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ are decay constant for two different processes, $N$ is the number of atoms. Now applying the decay law for the combined process, we get

$-\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda_{\text{eff}}N \dots(3)$

Equating equation (1) and (2) we get $\lambda_{\text{eff}} = (\lambda_1 + \lambda_2) \dots(4)$

Now the half life of the radioactive nucleus is given by, $\lambda = \frac{\ln(2)}{T} \dots(5)$ Where, $T$ is the half life of the radioactive nucleus. Using equation (5), equation (4) becomes,

$\frac{\ln(2)}{T} = \frac{\ln(2)}{T_1} + \frac{\ln(2)}{T_2} \implies \frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{T_1} + \frac{1}{T_2}$

$\frac{1}{T} = \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{100} = \frac{11}{100} \implies T = \frac{100}{11} \approx 9\text{ s}$

question_text:
A nucleus of mass $M$ emits $\gamma$-ray photon of frequency $v$. The loss of internal energy by the nucleus is:

[Take $c$ as the speed of electromagnetic wave]

Momentum of $\gamma$ ray $[P_{\gamma}] = \frac{h}{\lambda} = \frac{h v}{c}$

Total momentum is conserved.
$\vec{P}_{\gamma} + \vec{P}_{Nu} = 0$
where $\vec{P}_{Nu} =$ momentum of decayed nuclei
$\Rightarrow P_{\gamma} = P_{Nu}$
$\Rightarrow \frac{h v}{c} = P_{Nu}$
$\Rightarrow KE \text{ of nuclei}$

Loss in internal energy $= E_{\gamma} + KE_{Nu}$

If $f$ denotes the ratio of the number of nuclei decayed ($N_d$) to the number of nuclei at $t = 0$, ($N_0$) then for a collection of radioactive nuclei, the rate of change of $f$ with respect to time is given as:
[$\lambda$ is the radioactive decay constant]
solution:
$N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$

$N_d = N_0 - N$

$N_d = N_0\left(1 - e^{-\lambda t}\right)$

$\frac{N_d}{N_0} = f = 1 - e^{-\lambda t}$

$\frac{df}{dt} = \lambda e^{-\lambda t}$

question_text: At time $t = 0$, a material is composed of two radioactive atoms $A$ and $B$, where $N_A(0) = 2N_B(0)$. The decay constant of both kind of radioactive atoms is $\lambda$. However, $A$ disintegrates to $B$ and $B$ disintegrates to $C$. Which of the following figures represents the evolution of $\frac{N_B(t)}{N_B(0)}$ with respect to time $t$?
solution:
The rate at which nuclei of $B$ is forming,
$$\frac{dN_B}{dt} = \lambda N_A - \lambda N_B \implies \frac{dN_B}{dt} = 2\lambda N_{B0} e^{-\lambda t} - \lambda N_B$$
$$e^{\lambda t}\left(\frac{dN_B}{dt} + \lambda N_B\right) = 2\lambda N_{B0} \implies \frac{d}{dt}\left(N_B e^{\lambda t}\right) = 2\lambda N_{B0}$$
On integrating the above equation,
$$N_B e^{\lambda t} = 2\lambda N_{B0} t + C$$
At $t = 0$, $N_B = N_{B0} \implies C = N_{B0}$
$$N_B(t) = N_{B0}(1 + 2\lambda t)e^{-\lambda t} \implies \frac{N_B(t)}{N_{B}(0)} = (1 + 2\lambda t)e^{-\lambda t}$$
To find the maximum, set $\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{N_B(t)}{N_B(0)}\right) = 0$:
$$2\lambda e^{-\lambda t} - \lambda(1 + 2\lambda t)e^{-\lambda t} = 0$$
$$\lambda e^{-\lambda t}(1 - 2\lambda t) = 0 \implies t = \frac{1}{2\lambda}$$
Thus, the function starts at $1$ at $t = 0$, attains a maximum at $t = \frac{1}{2\lambda}$, and tends to $0$ as $t \to \infty$, which corresponds to figure (C).

question_text: There are $10^{10}$ radioactive nuclei in a given radioactive element. Its half-life time is $1\text{ min}$. How many nuclei will remain after $30\text{ s}$? $(\sqrt{2} = 1.414)$
solution:
Recall the relationship between the present amount of element and the initial amount of element in terms of the decay constant, $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, now the relation between decay constant and half-life, $t_{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{0.693}{\lambda}$

$$\Rightarrow N = N_0 e^{-\frac{0.693t}{t_{\frac{1}{2}}}}$$

$$\Rightarrow N = 10^{10} e^{-0.35} \approx 7 \times 10^9$$

Alternatively,
$$N = \frac{N_0}{2^{t/t_{1/2}}} = \frac{10^{10}}{2^{30/60}} = \frac{10^{10}}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{10^{10}}{1.414} \approx 7 \times 10^9$$

question_text: A sample of a radioactive nucleus $A$ disintegrates to another radioactive nucleus $B$, which in turn disintegrates to some other stable nucleus $C$. Plot of a graph showing the variation of number of atoms of nucleus $B$ versus time is : (Assume that at $t = 0$, there are no $B$ atoms in the sample)
solution:
No. of nuclei of $B$ is initially zero and finally zero. It will reach a maximum value at some intermediate time smoothly.
$$N_B(t) = \frac{\lambda_A N_0}{\lambda_B - \lambda_A} \left(e^{-\lambda_A t} - e^{-\lambda_B t}\right)$$
This function starts from zero, increases to a maximum, and then smoothly decays asymptotically to zero as $t \to \infty$, which corresponds to curve (C).

question_text: Nucleus $A$ is having mass number $220$ and its binding energy per nucleon is $5.6\text{ MeV}$. It splits in two fragments $B$ and $C$ of mass numbers $105$ and $115$. The binding energy of nucleons in $B$ and $C$ is $6.4\text{ MeV}$ per nucleon. The energy $Q$ released per fission will be:
solution:
The total binding energy of nucleus $A$ is,

$E_A = 220 \times 5.6 = 1232\text{ MeV}$

The total binding energy of $B$ and $C$ combined is,

$E_B + E_C = 105 \times 6.4 + 115 \times 6.4 = 1408\text{ MeV}$

Therefore, the energy released per fission is,

$Q = E_B + E_C - E_A = 1408 - 1232 = 176\text{ MeV}$

question_text: A sample contains $10^{-2}\text{ kg}$ each of two substances $A$ and $B$ with half lives $4\text{ s}$ and $8\text{ s}$ respectively. The ratio of their atomic weights is $1 : 2$. The ratio of the amounts of $A$ and $B$ after $16\text{ s}$ is $\frac{x}{100}$. The value of $x$ is _____.
solution:
Ratio of number of moles of substance in the beginning will be, $\frac{(N_0)_A}{(N_0)_B} = \frac{\frac{10^{-2}\text{ kg}}{M_A}}{\frac{10^{-2}\text{ kg}}{M_B}} = \frac{M_B}{M_A} = \frac{1}{2}$

Number of half-life in $16\text{ s}$ for element $A$ will be, $n_A = \frac{16}{4} = 4$

Number of half-life in $16\text{ s}$ for element $B$ will be, $n_B = \frac{16}{8} = 2$

Hence, ratio of number of nuclei after $16\text{ s}$ will be, $= \frac{(N_0)_A \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n_A}}{(N_0)_B \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{n_B}} = \frac{1}{2} \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{4-2} = \frac{1}{8} = \frac{25}{100}$

Thus, value of $x$ is $25$.

question_text: A radioactive nucleus can decay by two different processes. Half-life for the first process is $3.0\text{ hours}$ while it is $4.5\text{ hours}$ for the second process. The effective halflife of the nucleus will be
solution:
Here the particle is decayed by two processes with decay constant $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$.
Radioactive decay rate is directly proportional to number of nucleus present at any time, so total rate of decay is
$$\frac{dA}{dt} = -(\lambda_1 A) + (-\lambda_2 A) \Rightarrow \frac{dA}{dt} = -(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2) A \Rightarrow \lambda_{eff} = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2$$
$$\Rightarrow \frac{\ln 2}{\left(t_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)_{eff}} = \frac{\ln 2}{\left(t_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)_1} + \frac{(\ln 2)}{\left(t_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)_2} \Rightarrow \left(t_{\frac{1}{2}}\right)_{eff} = \frac{4.5 \times 3}{7.5}\text{ hours} = 1.8\text{ hours}$$

question_text:
Following statements related to radioactivity are given below :

(A) Radioactivity is a random and spontaneous process and is dependent on physical and chemical conditions.
(B) The number of undecayed nuclei in the radioactive sample decays exponentially with time.
(C) Slope of the graph of $\log_e (\text{no. of undecayed nuclei})$ vs. time represents the reciprocal of mean life time ($\tau$).
(D) Product of decay constant ($\lambda$) and half-life time ($T_{\frac{1}{2}}$) is not constant.

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
solution:
Radioactive decay is a random and spontaneous process, it depends on unbalancing of nucleus. This process is independent of physical and chemical conditions.

We know that, $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ ... (1), where $N = \text{number of undecayed nuclei in the sample at time } t$ and $N_0 = \text{initial number of nuclei}$.

This shows that the number of undecayed nuclei decays exponentially with time.

Taking log both sides of equation (1):
$$\ln N = -\lambda t + \ln N_0$$
So, $\text{magnitude of slope} = \lambda = \frac{1}{\tau}\text{ (reciprocal of mean life time)}$

Half-life time $T_{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$
Then,
$$\lambda \times T_{\frac{1}{2}} = \ln 2 = \text{constant}$$

Hence, (B) and (C) are correct only.

question_text: The activity of a radioactive material is $2.56 \times 10^{-3}\text{ Ci}$. If the half life of the material is $5\text{ days}$, after how many days the activity will become $2 \times 10^{-5}\text{ Ci}$?
solution:
The activity of a radioactive sample at any time $t$ is given by,
$$A = A_0 (2)^{-\frac{t}{T_{1/2}}}$$
$$\Rightarrow 2 \times 10^{-5} = 2.56 \times 10^{-3} \times 2^{-\frac{t}{5}}$$
$$\Rightarrow 2^{\frac{t}{5}} = \frac{2.56 \times 10^{-3}}{2 \times 10^{-5}} = 128 = 2^7$$
$$\Rightarrow \frac{t}{5} = 7 \implies t = 35\text{ days}$$

question_text:
In the following nuclear reaction,
$$D \xrightarrow{\alpha} D_1 \xrightarrow{\beta^-} D_2 \xrightarrow{\alpha} D_3 \xrightarrow{\gamma} D_4$$
Mass number of $D$ is $182$ and atomic number is $74$. Mass number and atomic number of $D_4$ respectively will be
solution:
Equivalent reaction can be written as:
$$D \to D_4 + 2\alpha + \beta^- + \gamma$$

So, mass number of $D_4 = \text{mass number of } D - 2 \times 4 = 182 - 8 = 174$

Atomic number of $D_4 = \text{atomic number of } D - 2 \times 2 + 1 = 74 - 4 + 1 = 71$

The step-by-step reaction is:
$$^{182}_{74}D \xrightarrow{\alpha} {^{178}_{72}D_1} \xrightarrow{\beta^-} {^{178}_{73}D_2} \xrightarrow{\alpha} {^{174}_{71}D_3} \xrightarrow{\gamma} {^{174}_{71}D_4}$$

question_text: The half life of a radioactive substance is $5\text{ years}$. After $x\text{ years}$ a given sample of the radioactive substance gets reduced to $6.25\%$ of its initial value. The value of $x$ is _____.
solution:
$6.25\%$ of the initial value means, final number of nuclei should be, $\left(\frac{N_0}{16}\right)$.

Number of nuclei remaining after $n$ half lives is $N = \frac{N_0}{2^n}$

$\frac{6.25}{100} N_0 = \frac{N_0}{2^n} \Rightarrow \frac{625}{10^4} = \frac{1}{2^n}$

$\Rightarrow 2^n = \frac{10^4}{5^4} \Rightarrow 2^n = 2^4$

$\Rightarrow n = 4$

Therefore, time taken will be, $n \times t_{\frac{1}{2}} = 4 \times 5 = 20\text{ years}$

question_text:
The disintegration rate of a certain radioactive sample at any instant is $4250\text{ disintegrations per minute}$. $10\text{ minutes}$ later, the rate becomes $2250\text{ disintegrations per minute}$. The approximate decay constant is
$(\text{Take } \log_e 1.88 = 0.63)$
solution:
At $t = 0$ disintegration rate $A_0 = 4250\text{ dpm}$

At $t = 10\text{ min}$ disintegration rate $A_t = 2250\text{ dpm}$

The activity of a sample at any time is given by,
$A_t = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$

$\Rightarrow 2250 = 4250 e^{-\lambda(10)}$

$\Rightarrow 10\lambda = \ln\left(\frac{4250}{2250}\right) = \ln 1.88$

$\Rightarrow \lambda = 0.063\text{ min}^{-1}$

question_text: Mass numbers of two nuclei are in the ratio of $4 : 3$. Their nuclear densities will be in the ratio of
solution:
Radius of nucleus
$R = R_0 A^{\frac{1}{3}}$

$\text{Density of nucleus } (\rho) = \frac{\text{Mass of nucleus}}{\text{volume of nucleus}}$

$\rho = \frac{m \times A}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}$ Where $m$: mass of proton or neutron and $A$: mass number.

$\Rightarrow \rho = \frac{m \times A}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A}$

$\Rightarrow \rho \propto A^0$

Hence, density of nucleus is independent of mass number.

Therefore, the ratio is $1 : 1$.

Two lighter nuclei combine to form a comparatively heavier nucleus by the relation given below:

The binding energies per nucleon of $_{1}^{2}X$ and $_{2}^{4}Y$ are $1.1\text{ MeV}$ and $7.6\text{ MeV}$ respectively. The energy released in this process is _____ $\text{MeV}$.

question_text: What is the half-life period of a radioactive material if its activity drops to $\frac{1}{16^{\text{th}}}$ of its initial value of 30 years ?
solution:
Activity of a radioactive material is given by $A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, here, $\lambda$ is decay constant.
Taking logarithmic function both sides,
$\Rightarrow -\lambda t = \ln \left(\frac{A}{A_0}\right)$
Using relation between half life and decay constant,
$\Rightarrow -\frac{\ln 2}{t_{\frac{1}{2}}} \times 30 = \ln \left(\frac{1}{16}\right)$
$\Rightarrow -\frac{\ln 2}{t_{\frac{1}{2}}} \times 30 = -4 \ln 2$
$\Rightarrow t_{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{30}{4} = 7.5\text{ yrs}$

question_text: The activity of a radioactive material is $6.4 \times 10^{-4}\text{ curie}$. Its half life is $5\text{ days}$. The activity will become $5 \times 10^{-6}\text{ curie}$ after

question_text: A freshly prepared radioactive source of half life $2\text{ hours } 30\text{ minutes}$ emits radiation which is $64\text{ times}$ the permissible safe level. The minimum time, after which it would be possible to work safely with source, will be _____ $\text{hours}$.

Using radioactive decay law relation,

Putting the values, we have
$x = 64x \times 2^{-\frac{t}{T}}$
$\therefore t = 6T = 6 \times 2.5 = 15\text{ hours}$

question_text: A radioactive sample decays $\frac{7}{8}\text{ times}$ its original quantity in $15\text{ minutes}$. The half-life of the sample is
solution:
Remaining amount of sample is $= 1 - \frac{7}{8} = \frac{1}{8}$

Using radioactive decay law
$$N = N_0(2)^{-\frac{t}{T_{\frac{1}{2}}}}$$

We have,
$$(2)^{\frac{t}{T_{\frac{1}{2}}}} = \frac{N_0}{N} = \frac{N_0}{\frac{N_0}{8}} = 8 = (2)^3$$

Then, $\frac{t}{T_{\frac{1}{2}}} = 3$

Thus, half life of the sample is $T_{\frac{1}{2}} = 5\text{ min}$

question_text:
Read the following statements:
(A) Volume of the nucleus is directly proportional to the mass number.
(B) Volume of the nucleus is independent of mass number.
(C) Density of the nucleus is directly proportional to the mass number.
(D) Density of the nucleus is directly proportional to the cube root of the mass number.
(E) Density of the nucleus is independent of the mass number.

Choose the correct option from the following options.
solution:
Radius of nucleus is
$$R = R_0 A^{\frac{1}{3}}$$, where, $R_0 = 1.2 \times 10^{-15}\text{ m}$ and $A$ is mass number of nucleus.

Thus, $R \propto A^{\frac{1}{3}}$

Volume of nucleus is $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \Rightarrow V \propto R^3 \Rightarrow V \propto A$.

Now, the density of nucleus is given by $\rho = \frac{M}{V} = \frac{mA}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \frac{m}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3}$

Thus, density is independent of $A$.

Hence, only (A) and (E) are correct.

question_text: Two radioactive materials $A$ and $B$ have decay constants $25\lambda$ and $16\lambda$ respectively. If initially they have the same number of nuclei, then the ratio of the number of nuclei of $B$ to that of $A$ will be "$e$" after a time $\frac{1}{a\lambda}$. The value of $a$ is ______.
solution:
According to radioactive decay formula, $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, here, $N_0$ is the initial number of nuclei in a radioactive material.
Given here, $\lambda_1 = 25\lambda$ and $\lambda_2 = 16\lambda$.
And $\frac{N_B}{N_A} = e$
For radioactive material $A$, $N_A = N_0 e^{-\lambda_1 t}$
For radioactive material $B$, $N_B = N_0 e^{-\lambda_2 t}$
Thus, the ratio $\frac{N_B}{N_A} = \frac{e^{-\lambda_2 t}}{e^{-\lambda_1 t}} = e^{-\lambda_2 t} \cdot e^{\lambda_1 t}$
$\Rightarrow e^1 = e^{(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)t}$
$\Rightarrow (\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)t = 1$
Time, $t = \frac{1}{\lambda_1 - \lambda_2} = \frac{1}{25\lambda - 16\lambda} = \frac{1}{9\lambda}$.
Hence, the value of $a = 9$.

question_text: Assume that protons and neutrons have equal masses. Mass of a nucleon is $1.6 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$ and radius of nucleus is $1.5 \times 10^{-15} A^{\frac{1}{3}}\text{ m}$. The approximate ratio of the nuclear density and water density is $n \times 10^{13}$. The value of $n$ is ______.
solution:
As we know, $\text{density of nuclei} = \frac{\text{mass of nuclei}}{\text{volume of nuclei}}$
$\Rightarrow \rho = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-27} A}{\frac{4}{3}\pi (1.5 \times 10^{-15})^3 A}$
$= \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-27}}{14.14 \times 10^{-45}} = 0.113 \times 10^{18}\text{ kg m}^{-3}$
We also know that, density of water is $\rho_w = 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}$.
Hence,
$\frac{\rho}{\rho_w} = 11.31 \times 10^{13}$.
Therefore, $n \approx 11$

question_text:
Consider the following radioactive decay process:
$^{218}_{84}\text{A} \xrightarrow{\alpha} \text{A}_1 \xrightarrow{\beta^-} \text{A}_2 \xrightarrow{\gamma} \text{A}_3 \xrightarrow{\alpha} \text{A}_4 \xrightarrow{\beta^+} \text{A}_5 \xrightarrow{\gamma} \text{A}_6$
The mass number and the atomic number of $\text{A}_6$ are given by:
solution:
When an alpha particle is emitted from nucleus the nucleus loses two proton and two neutrons. This means the atomic mass number decreases by $4$ and the atomic number decreases by $2$.
In beta decays, the mass number of the atoms remains the same, but the atomic number changes: the atomic number increases in the negative beta decay and decreases in the positive beta decay by $1$, respectively.
In gamma decay, mass number and atomic number remains unchanged.
Step by step variation is given below:
$^{218}_{84}\text{A} \xrightarrow{\alpha} {}^{214}_{82}\text{A}_1 \xrightarrow{\beta^-} {}^{214}_{83}\text{A}_2 \xrightarrow{\gamma} {}^{214}_{83}\text{A}_3 \xrightarrow{\alpha} {}^{210}_{81}\text{A}_4 \xrightarrow{\beta^+} {}^{210}_{80}\text{A}_5 \xrightarrow{\gamma} {}^{210}_{80}\text{A}_6$

question_text:
The energy released per fission of nucleus of $\text{X}240$ is $200\text{ MeV}$. The energy released if all the atoms in $120\text{ g}$ of pure $\text{X}240$ undergo fission is _____ $\times 10^{25}\text{ MeV}$.

(Given $N_A = 6 \times 10^{23}$)
solution:
Energy released per fission is $200\text{ MeV}$.

The number of atoms $n$ in $120\text{ g}$:
$$n = \frac{120}{240} \times 6 \times 10^{23}\text{ atoms}.$$

Total energy released, $E = n \times 200\text{ MeV}$
$$= \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 10^{23} \times 200 = 600 \times 10^{23}\text{ MeV} = 6 \times 10^{25}\text{ MeV}$$

question_text: The ratio of the density of oxygen nucleus $(\text{O}816)$ and helium nucleus $(\text{He}24)$ is
solution:
The radius of a nucleus, $R$ is related to its mass number $A$ as:
$$R = R_0 A^{\frac{1}{3}}$$
where $R_0$ is the nuclear radius of hydrogen.

Thus, the density of a nucleus is given by:
$$d = \frac{\mu A}{\frac{4}{3}\pi \left(R_0 A^{\frac{1}{3}}\right)^3} = \frac{3\mu}{4\pi R_0^3} = \text{Constant}$$

Hence, the ratio of nuclear density of oxygen to helium nucleus is $1 : 1$

question_text: A radioactive element $\text{X}92242$ emits two $\alpha$-particles, one electron and two positrons. The product nucleus is represented by $\text{Y}P234$. The value of $P$ is _____.
solution:
When a radioactive nucleus emits $1\alpha$-particle, its mass number decreases by $4$ and the atomic number decreases by $2$. During positron emission, the mass number remains unchanged but the atomic number decreases by $1$. Similarly, during electron emission, the mass number remains unchanged but the atomic number increases by $1$.

So, the value of $P = 92 - 2(2) + 1 - 2(1) = 92 - 4 + 1 - 2 = 92 - 2 - 2 + 1 - 1 - 1$
$$\Rightarrow P = 92 - 5$$
$$\Rightarrow P = 87.$$

question_text: If a radioactive element having half-life of $30\text{ min}$ is undergoing beta decay, the fraction of radioactive element remains undecayed after $90\text{ min}$ will be :
solution:
Given: Half life of radioactive element $t_{\frac{1}{2}} = 30\text{ min}$

In $90\text{ min}$, there will be three half lives, so $n = 3$.

Using radioactive decay law, fraction of radioactive element remains undecayed is
$$\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3$$
$$\Rightarrow \frac{N}{N_0} = \frac{1}{8}$$

question_text: Substance $A$ has atomic mass number 16 and half life of 1 day. Another substance $B$ has atomic mass number 32 and half life of $\frac{1}{2}\text{ day}$. If both $A$ and $B$ simultaneously start undergo radio activity at the same time with initial mass $320\text{ g}$ each, how many total atoms of $A$ and $B$ combined would be left after 2 days
solution:
Number of nuclei left after $n$ half-lives is given by,
$$N = N_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{t}{t_{1/2}}}$$

As, $(N_0)_A = \frac{320}{16} = 20\text{ moles}$ and
$(N_0)_B = \frac{320}{32} = 10\text{ moles}$

Then, $N_A = \frac{(N_0)_A}{(2)^2} = \frac{20}{4} = 5$ and
$N_B = \frac{(N_0)_B}{(2)^{\frac{2}{0.5}}} = \frac{10}{2^4} = 0.625$

So total $N = 5 + 0.625 = 5.625\text{ moles}$
and number of atoms $= 5.625 \times 6.023 \times 10^{23} = 3.38 \times 10^{24}$

question_text:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R

Assertion A : The nuclear density of nuclides ${}_{5}^{10}\text{B}, {}_{3}^{6}\text{Li}, {}_{26}^{56}\text{Fe}, {}_{10}^{20}\text{Ne}$ and ${}_{83}^{209}\text{Bi}$ can be arranged as $\rho_{\text{Bi}}^N > \rho_{\text{Fe}}^N > \rho_{\text{Ne}}^N > \rho_{\text{B}}^N > \rho_{\text{Li}}^N$

Reason R : The radius $R$ of nucleus is related to its mass number $A$ as $R = R_0 A^{\frac{1}{3}}$, where $R_0$ is a constant.

In the light of the above statement, choose the correct answer from the options given below :

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

solution:
Nuclear density is given by, $\rho = \frac{m}{\frac{4}{3}\pi (R_0)^3}$, where $m$ is mass of proton. Clearly it is independent of $A$ and same for all nucleus.

Radius of the nucleus is given by, $R = R_0 A^{\frac{1}{3}}$

question_text:
A radioactive nucleus decays by two different process. The half life of the first process is $5\text{ minutes}$ and that of the second process is $30\text{ s}$. The effective half-life of the nucleus is calculated to be $\frac{\alpha}{11}\text{ s}$.
The value of $\alpha$ is _____.
solution:
Decay law for both process can be written as,
$$\frac{dN_1}{dt} = -\lambda_1 N \dots \text{Eq}(1) \text{ and}$$
$$\frac{dN_2}{dt} = -\lambda_2 N \dots \text{Eq}(2)$$
Hence, net decay will become
$$\frac{dN}{dt} = \frac{dN_1}{dt} + \frac{dN_2}{dt} = -(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)N$$
$$\Rightarrow \lambda_{eq} = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2$$
$$\Rightarrow \frac{\ln 2}{t_{\frac{1}{2}}} = \frac{\ln 2}{300} + \frac{\ln 2}{30}$$
$$\Rightarrow t_{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{300}{11}$$
Hence, required value of $\alpha = 300$.

question_text: The mass of proton, neutron and helium nucleus are respectively $1.0073\text{u}$, $1.0087\text{u}$ and $4.0015\text{u}$. The binding energy of helium nucleus is:
solution:
Given here, $m_{\text{He}} = 4.0015\text{u}$, $m_p = 1.0073\text{u}$ and $m_n = 1.0087\text{u}$.
Mass defect
$$\Delta m = 2m_p + 2m_n - m_{\text{He}} = 2 \times 1.0073 + 2 \times 1.0087 - 4.0015 = 0.0305\text{u}$$
Binding energy
$$E = \Delta m \times 931\text{ MeV} = 0.0305 \times 931 = 28.4\text{ MeV}$$

question_text: Nucleus $A$ having $Z = 17$ and equal number of protons and neutrons has $1.2\text{ MeV}$ binding energy per nucleon. Another nucleus $B$ of $Z = 12$ has total 26 nucleons and $1.8\text{ MeV}$ binding energy per nucleons. The difference of binding energy of $B$ and $A$ will be _____ $\text{MeV}$.
solution:
In $A$, $Z = 17$ and have equal numbers of protons and neutrons i.e. $\text{nucleons} = 2 \times 17 = 34$
So, for $A$,
Total binding energy $BE_A = 1.2 \times 34 = 40.8\text{ MeV}$
Another nucleus $B$ mass number $= 26$
So, total binding energy of $B$ is $BE_B = 1.8 \times 26\text{ MeV} = 46.8\text{ MeV}$
Difference of $BE = BE_B - BE_A = 6\text{ MeV}$

question_text: A nucleus with mass number 242 and binding energy per nucleon as $7.6\text{ MeV}$ breaks into two fragment each with mass number 121. If each fragment nucleus has binding energy per nucleon as $8.1\text{ MeV}$, the total gain in binding energy is _____ $\text{MeV}$.
solution: Binding energy is given by $E = \Delta mc^2$ where $\Delta m$ is the mass defect. The energy per nucleon of the nucleus having mass number 242 is $7.6\text{ MeV}$. The initial binding energy is, $BE = 242 \times 7.6\text{ MeV}$. The energy per nucleon of the nucleus with mass number 121 is $8.1\text{ MeV}$. Therefore, binding energy is $BE$ $(121 \times 8.1\text{ MeV})$. The gain in the binding energy is $BE = 121\text{ MeV}$.

question_text:
For a nucleus $X_Z^A$ having mass number $A$ and atomic number $Z$

A. The surface energy per nucleon $(b_s) = -a_1 A^{-\frac{2}{3}}$.

B. The Coulomb contribution to the binding energy $b_c = -a_2 \frac{Z(Z-1)}{A^{\frac{4}{3}}}$.

C. The volume energy $b_v = a_3 A$

D. Decrease in the binding energy is proportional to surface area.

E. While estimating the surface energy, it is assumed that each nucleon interacts with 12 nucleons. ($a_1, a_2$ and $a_3$ are constants)

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
solution:
The formula to calculate the radius of a nucleus is given by
$$R = R_0 A^{\frac{1}{3}} \quad \dots (1)$$
Hence, the volume energy can be written as
$$b_v = C_1 R^3 = a_3 \left(A^{\frac{1}{3}}\right)^3 = a_3 A$$
The nuclear binding energy is the minimum energy that is required to disassemble the nucleus of an atom into its constituent protons and neutrons. Also, the energy of the nucleus is negative with regard to the energy of the particles pulled apart to infinite distance, because energy must be utilised to split a nucleus into its individual protons and neutrons. It is proportional to the surface area.
Hence, statements C and D are most appropriate.

question_text: A radio active material is reduced to $\frac{1}{8}$ of its original amount in $3\text{ days}$. If $8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg}$ of the material is left after $5\text{ days}$ the initial amount of the material is
solution:
The initial and final amount of the radioactive substance are related by the formula
$$\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n \quad \dots (1)$$
where, $n$ is the number of half lives.
Substitute $\frac{1}{8}$ for $\frac{N}{N_0}$ into equation (1) and solve to calculate the value of $n$.
$$\frac{1}{8} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n \implies \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n \implies n = 3$$
The half-life of the radioactive element can be calculated as follows:
$$\frac{t}{t_{1/2}} = n \quad \dots (2)$$
Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (2) and solve to calculate the half-life.
$$\frac{3\text{ days}}{t_{1/2}} = 3 \implies t_{1/2} = 1\text{ day}$$
The initial and the final mass of the radioactive element are related by
$$\frac{m}{m_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{t'}{t_{1/2}}} \quad \dots (3)$$
Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (3) and solve to calculate the initial mass of the substance.
$$\frac{8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg}}{m_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{5}{1}} \implies m_0 = 2^5 \times 8 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg} = 256\text{ g}$$

question_text: The decay constant for a radioactive nuclide is $1.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ s}^{-1}$. Atomic weight of the substance is $60\text{ g}\text{ mole}^{-1}$, $N_A = 6 \times 10^{23}$. The activity of $1.0\mu\text{g}$ of the substance is $\underline{\hspace{1cm}} \times 10^{10}\text{ Bq}$.
solution:
It is given that
$\lambda = 1.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ s}^{-1}$

Number of moles is $\frac{1 \times 10^{-6}}{60} = \frac{10^{-7}}{6}$

Number of atoms $=$ number of moles $\times N_A$
$N_0 = \frac{10^{-7}}{6} \times 6 \times 10^{23} = 10^{16}$

Hence, at $t = 0$, $A = A_0 = N_0\lambda$, the activity can be given by
$A = N_0\lambda e^{-\lambda t} \Rightarrow A = 10^{16} \times 1.5 \times 10^{-5} \times 1 = 15 \times 10^{10}\text{ Bq}$

question_text: The half life of a radioactive substance is $T$. The time taken, for disintegrating $\left(\frac{7}{8}\right)^{\text{th}}$ part of its original mass will be:
solution:
It is given that $t_{\frac{1}{2}} = T$

After disintegration of $\left(\frac{7}{8}\right)^{\text{th}}$ part, $\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^{\text{th}}$ part is only left.

Using the decay formula,
$N = N_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{t}{t_{1/2}}}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{N_0}{8} = N_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{t}{T}} \Rightarrow -\ln 8 = -\frac{t}{T} \ln 2 \Rightarrow 3 \ln 2 = \frac{t}{T} \ln 2 \Rightarrow t = 3T$

question_text: Two radioactive elements $A$ and $B$ initially have same number of atoms. The half life of $A$ is same as the average life of $B$. If $\lambda_A$ and $\lambda_B$ are decay constants of $A$ and $B$ respectively, then choose the correct relation from the given options.
solution:
It is given that
$T_{\frac{1}{2}}(A) = T_{av}(B)$

The half life of a substance is given by $T_{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$

So,
$\frac{\ln 2}{\lambda_A} = \frac{1}{\lambda_B}$

$\Rightarrow \lambda_A = \lambda_B \ln 2$

question_text:
A common example of alpha decay is
$^{238}_{92}\text{U} \to ^{234}_{90}\text{Th} + ^4_2\text{He} + Q$

Given:
$^{238}_{92}\text{U} = 238.05060\text{u}$
$^{234}_{90}\text{Th} = 234.04360\text{u}$
$^4_2\text{He} = 4.00260\text{u}$ and $1\text{u} = 931.5\frac{\text{MeV}}{c^2}$

The energy released ($Q$) during the alpha decay of $^{238}_{92}\text{U}$ is $\underline{\hspace{1cm}}\text{ MeV}$.
solution:
The formula to calculate the Q-value of the given nuclear reaction can be written as
$Q = (m_U - m_{Th} - m_{He})c^2$ ... (1)

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (1) to calculate the required Q-value for the reaction.
$Q = (238.05060\text{u} - 234.04360\text{u} - 4.00260\text{u})c^2$
$= 0.0044c^2 \times 931.5\text{MeV}/c^2$
$\approx 4\text{MeV}$

question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R

Assertion A : The binding energy per nucleon is practically independent of the atomic number for nuclei of mass number in the range 30 to 170.

Reason R : Nuclear force is short ranged.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false.

solution:
The binding energy for stable nuclei is always a positive number, as the nucleus must gain energy for the nucleons to move apart from each other. Nucleons are attracted to each other by the strong nuclear force. Binding energy per nucleon is almost constant in the range of $30 - 170$. This is because nuclear energy is a short range force. It operates in the femto metre region.
Hence, this option is the correct one.

question_text: The half-life of a radioactive nucleus is 5 years. The fraction of the original sample that would decay in 15 years is :
solution:
The formula to calculate the number of half lives covered by the radioactive material is given by
$n = \frac{t}{T_{\frac{1}{2}}} \dots (1)$

Substitute the values of the known parameters into equation (1) to calculate the number of half lives covered.
$n = \frac{15\,\text{years}}{5\,\text{years}} = 3$

The relation between the amount of radioactive substance after certain time can be written as
$N = N_0 2^{-n} \dots (2)$

Substitute the value of $n$ into equation (2) to obtain the fraction of the remaining substance.
$N = N_0 2^{-3} \Rightarrow \frac{N}{N_0} = \frac{1}{8}$

Hence, the amount of the decayed substance can be written as
$1 - \frac{N}{N_0} = 1 - \frac{1}{8} = \frac{7}{8}$

question_text: In a nuclear fission process, a high mass nuclide ($A \approx 236$) with binding energy $7.6\,\text{MeV}/\text{Nucleon}$ dissociated into two middle mass nuclides ($A \approx 118$), having binding energy of $8.6\,\text{MeV}/\text{Nucleon}$. The energy released in the process would be _____ $\text{MeV}$.
solution:
The formula to calculate the energy released in the given process can be written as
$Q = \text{BE}_{\text{Product}} - \text{BE}_{\text{Reactant}} \dots (1)$

From equation (1), it follows that
$Q = 2(118)(8.6) - 236(7.6)\,\text{MeV} = 236\,\text{MeV}$

question_text: The atomic mass of $^{12}_{6}\text{C}$ is $12.000000u$ and that of $^{13}_{6}\text{C}$ is $13.003354u$. The required energy to remove a neutron from $^{13}_{6}\text{C}$, if mass of neutron is $1.008665u$, will be:

The mass defect for the above reaction can be calculated as follows:

$$= -0.00531\text{ u}$$

Hence, the energy required is given by
$$E = 0.00531 \times 931.5\text{ MeV}$$
$$= 4.95\text{ MeV}$$

question_text:
The explosive in a Hydrogen bomb is a mixture of $^{2}_{1}\text{H}$, $^{3}_{1}\text{H}$ and $^{6}_{3}\text{Li}$ in some condensed form. The chain reaction is given by $^{6}_{3}\text{Li} + {^{1}_{0}\text{n}} \rightarrow {^{4}_{2}\text{He}} + {^{3}_{1}\text{H}}$; $^{2}_{1}\text{H} + {^{3}_{1}\text{H}} \rightarrow {^{4}_{2}\text{He}} + {^{1}_{0}\text{n}}$ During the explosion the energy released is approximately
$$\left[\text{Given }: M(\text{Li}) = 6.01690\text{ amu},\, M\left({^{2}_{1}\text{H}}\right) = 2.01471\text{ amu},\, M\left({^{4}_{2}\text{He}}\right) = 4.00388\text{ amu} \text{ and } 1\text{amu} = 931.5\text{ MeV}\right]$$
solution:
Combining the reactions, it can be written that
$^{6}_{3}\text{Li} + {^{1}_{0}\text{n}} \rightarrow {^{4}_{2}\text{He}} + {^{3}_{1}\text{H}}$
$^{2}_{1}\text{H} + {^{3}_{1}\text{H}} \rightarrow {^{4}_{2}\text{He}} + {^{1}_{0}\text{n}}$
$\overline{^{6}_{3}\text{Li} + {^{2}_{1}\text{H}} \rightarrow 2\left({^{4}_{2}\text{He}}\right)}$

Hence, the energy released in process can be calculated as follows
$$Q = \Delta mc^2$$
$$= [M(\text{Li}) + M({^{2}_{1}\text{H}}) - 2 \times M({^{4}_{2}\text{He}})] \times 931.5\text{ MeV}$$
$$= [6.01690 + 2.01471 - 2 \times 4.00388] \times 931.5\text{ MeV}$$
$$= 22.22\text{ MeV}$$

question_text: In a nuclear fission reaction of an isotope of mass $M$, three similar daughter nuclei of same mass are formed. The speed of a daughter nuclei in terms of mass defect $\Delta M$ will be :
solution:
Let the reaction be, $(P) \rightarrow (X) + (Y) + (Z)$

Let mass of each daughter nuclei be $m$, then mass defect can be written as $\Delta M = M - 3m$.

Now the energy released will be in the form of kinetic energy of the daughter nuclei. Therefore,
$$\Delta M c^2 = \frac{1}{2}m V^2 + \frac{1}{2}m V^2 + \frac{1}{2}m V^2 \Rightarrow V = \sqrt{\frac{2\Delta M c^2}{3m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\Delta M c^2}{M - \Delta M}} \approx c\sqrt{\frac{2\Delta M}{M}}$$

question_text: A nucleus has mass number $A_1$ and volume $V_1$. Another nucleus has mass number $A_2$ and volume $V_2$. If relation between mass number is $A_2 = 4A_1$, then $\frac{V_2}{V_1} = \underline{\hspace{1cm}}$.
solution:
For a nucleus we can write volume: $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3$

Now, $R = R_0 (A)^{\frac{1}{3}}$

Therefore, $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A$
$$\Rightarrow \frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{A_2}{A_1} = 4$$

question_text: The mass number of nucleus having radius equal to half of the radius of nucleus with mass number $192$ is:

Therefore, we can write $R_0(A_1)^{1/3} = \frac{R_0}{2}(A_2)^{1/3}$

$\Rightarrow A_1 = \frac{1}{8} A_2$

question_text: The radius of a nucleus of mass number $64$ is $4.8\text{ fermi}$. Then the mass number of another nucleus having radius of $4\text{ fermi}$ is $\frac{1000}{x}$, where $x$ is ______.
solution:
Radius of a nucleus is given by, $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$.

Therefore, $R^3 \propto A$

$\Rightarrow \left(\frac{4.8}{4}\right)^3 = \frac{64}{A}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{64}{A} = (1.2)^3$

$\Rightarrow \frac{64}{A} = 1.44 \times 1.2$

$\Rightarrow A = \frac{64}{1.44 \times 1.2} = \frac{1000}{x}$

$\Rightarrow x = \frac{144 \times 12}{64} = 27$

question_text:
From the statements given below:

(A) The angular momentum of an electron in $n^{\text{th}}$ orbit is an integral multiple of $h$.
(B) Nuclear forces do not obey inverse square law.
(C) Nuclear forces are spin dependent.
(D) Nuclear forces are central and charge independent.
(E) Stability of nucleus is inversely proportional to the value of packing fraction.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
solution:
(A) Electron revolves around nucleus only in those orbits for which the angular momentum is an integral multiple of $\frac{h}{2\pi}$.
(B) Nuclear force does not follow the inverse square law.
(C) Nuclear forces are spin dependent but charge independent.
(D) Nuclear force is attractive in nature. It is a non central force, meaning it does not depend upon the distance between the particles but rather upon their orientation. Nuclear force is stronger if the spin is parallel; and weak if it is anti parallel.
(E) The negative value (less quantity) of packing fraction indicates that the isotope is stable. Positive value of packing fraction implies unstable (radioactive) nucleus. Also, the stability of the nucleus is inversely proportional to the value of the packing fraction.

question_text:
The disintegration energy $Q$ for the nuclear fission of $^{235}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{140}\text{Ce} + {}^{94}\text{Zr} + n$ is $\underline{\hspace{1cm}}\text{ MeV}$.
Given atomic masses of $^{235}\text{U} : 235.0439\text{u}$; $^{140}\text{Ce} : 139.9054\text{u}$, $^{94}\text{Zr} : 93.9063\text{u}$; $n : 1.0086\text{u}$, Value of $c^2 = 931\text{MeV/u}$
solution:
$^{235}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{140}\text{Ce} + {}^{94}\text{Zr} + n$

Disintegration energy:
$$\begin{aligned}
Q &= (m_R - m_P)c^2 \\
m_R &= 235.0439\text{ u} \\
m_P &= 139.9054\text{ u} + 93.9063\text{ u} + 1.0086\text{ u} \\
&= 234.8203\text{ u} \\
Q &= (235.0439\text{ u} - 234.8203\text{ u})c^2 \\
&= 0.2236\text{ u} \cdot c^2 \\
&= 0.2236 \times 931\text{ MeV} \\
Q &= 208.1716\text{ MeV} \approx 208\text{ MeV}
\end{aligned}$$

question_text:
A star has $100\%$ helium composition. It starts to convert three $^4\text{He}$ into one $^{12}\text{C}$ via triple alpha process as $^4\text{He} + {}^4\text{He} + {}^4\text{He} \rightarrow {}^{12}\text{C} + Q$. The mass of the star is $2.0 \times 10^{32}\text{ kg}$ and it generates energy at the rate of $5.808 \times 10^{30}\text{ W}$. The rate of converting these $^4\text{He}$ to $^{12}\text{C}$ is $n \times 10^{42}\text{ s}^{-1}$, where $n$ is ______
[ Take, mass of $^4\text{He} = 4.0026\text{u}$, mass of $^{12}\text{C} = 12\text{u}$ ]
solution:
$^4\text{He} + {}^4\text{He} + {}^4\text{He} \rightarrow {}^{12}\text{C} + Q$
$$\text{power generated} = \frac{N}{t} Q$$
where, $\frac{N}{t} \rightarrow \text{No. of reaction /sec.}$
$$Q = (3\text{ m}_{\text{He}} - m_{\text{C}}) c^2$$
$$Q = (3 \times 4.0026 - 12) \times 931.5\text{ MeV} \approx 7.266\text{ MeV}$$
$$\frac{N}{t} = \frac{\text{power}}{Q} = \frac{5.808 \times 10^{30}}{7.266 \times 10^6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}$$
$$\frac{N}{t} = 5 \times 10^{42}$$
rate of conversion of $^4\text{He}$ into $^{12}\text{C} = 3 \times \frac{N}{t} = 15 \times 10^{42}$
Hence, $n = 15$

question_text: A nucleus at rest disintegrates into two smaller nuclei with their masses in the ratio of $2 : 1$. After disintegration they will move :

options.text: in the same direction with same speed.
in opposite directions with the same speed.
in opposite directions with speed in the ratio of $2 : 1$ respectively.
in opposite directions with speed in the ratio of $1 : 2$ respectively.

solution:
By conservation of momentum:
$$P_i = P_f$$
$$0 = m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2$$
$$m_1 u_1 = -m_2 u_2$$
$$\frac{u_1}{u_2} = -\frac{m_2}{m_1}$$
Given $\frac{m_1}{m_2} = \frac{2}{1}$:
$$\frac{u_1}{u_2} = -\frac{1}{2}$$
This indicates that the two objects move in opposite directions with a speed ratio of $1:2$.

$\&$

question_text: A radioactive nucleus $n_2$ has 3 times the decay constant as compared to the decay constant of another radioactive nucleus $n_1$. If initial number of both nuclei are the same, what is the ratio of number of nuclei of $n_2$ to the number of nuclei of $n_1$, after one half-life of $n_1$ ?
solution:
$N_2 = N_0 e^{-3\lambda t}$
$N_1 = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$
$\frac{N_2}{N_1} = e^{-2\lambda t}$

$t_{\text{half life of } n_1} = t = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$

$\frac{N_0}{2} = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$
$\lambda t = \ln 2$
$t = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$

$\frac{N_2}{N_1} = e^{-2\lambda \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}} = e^{-2 \ln 2} = \frac{1}{4}$

question_text: A radioactive material $\text{P}$ first decays into $\text{Q}$ and then $\text{Q}$ decays to non-radioactive material $\text{R}$. Which of the following figure represents time dependent mass of $\text{P}$, $\text{Q}$ and $\text{R}$?
solution:
For the radioactive decay chain:
$$\text{P} \xrightarrow{\lambda_1} \text{Q} \xrightarrow{\lambda_2} \text{R}$$
where $\text{R}$ is a stable (non-radioactive) nucleus:

1. The mass of parent nucleus $\text{P}$ decreases exponentially with time:
$$N_{\text{P}}(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda_1 t}$$

2. The mass of daughter nucleus $\text{Q}$ starts at zero, increases to a maximum, and then decreases asymptotically to zero:
$$N_{\text{Q}}(t) = \frac{\lambda_1 N_0}{\lambda_2 - \lambda_1} \left(e^{-\lambda_1 t} - e^{-\lambda_2 t}\right)$$

3. The mass of stable end-product $\text{R}$ starts at zero and monotonically increases with time, asymptotically approaching $N_0$ as $t \to \infty$:
$$N_{\text{R}}(t) = N_0 - N_{\text{P}}(t) - N_{\text{Q}}(t)$$

Therefore, graph (B) correctly represents the variation of mass of $\text{P}$, $\text{Q}$, and $\text{R}$ with time.

question_text: For a nucleus of mass number $A$ and radius $R$, the mass density of nucleus can be represented as
solution:
The mass density ($\rho$) of a nucleus is defined as the ratio of its mass to its volume:
$$\rho = \frac{\text{Mass of nucleus}}{\text{Volume of nucleus}}$$

For a spherical nucleus with radius $R$, the volume is:
$$\text{Volume} = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3$$

The mass of the nucleus is related to the mass number $A$:
$$\text{Mass} = A \times m_u \text{ (where } m_u \text{ is the atomic mass unit, approximately } 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg)}$$

Therefore:
$$\rho = \frac{A \times m_u}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}$$

Now, there's an important relationship between the mass number $A$ and nuclear radius $R$. Empirically, it has been found that:
$$R = R_0 \times A^{1/3}$$

Where $R_0$ is a constant approximately equal to $1.2 \times 10^{-15}\text{ m}$ (1.2 fermi). Substituting this into the density equation:
$$\rho = \frac{A \times m_u}{\frac{4}{3}\pi (R_0 \times A^{1/3})^3}$$
$$\rho = \frac{A \times m_u}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 \times A}$$
$$\rho = \frac{m_u}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3}$$

This shows that the nuclear density is approximately constant for all nuclei, regardless of their mass number. This is a fundamental property of nuclear matter known as nuclear saturation density. The numerical value is:
$$\rho = 2.3 \times 10^{17}\text{ kg/m}^3$$

question_text:
$7.9\text{ MeV}$ $\alpha$-particle scatters from a target material of atomic number $79$. From the given data the estimated diameter of nuclei of the target material is (approximately) $\text{______ m}$.
$\left[\frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9\text{ N}\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2\text{ and electron charge} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}\right]$
solution:
For Rutherford scattering, at the closest approach all kinetic energy converts to electrostatic potential energy. For alpha particle-nucleus collision:
$$\text{K.E.} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \frac{Z_1 Z_2 e^2}{r_{\text{min}}}$$
Where: $Z_1 = 2$ (alpha), $Z_2 = 79$ (gold), $\text{K.E.} = 7.9\text{ MeV}$
$$r_{\text{min}} = \frac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 79 \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})^2}{7.9 \times 10^6 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}$$
$$r_{\text{min}} = 2.88 \times 10^{-14}\text{ m}$$
The estimated nuclear diameter is approximately:
$$d = 2 \times r_{\text{min}} = 5.76 \times 10^{-14}\text{ m}$$

question_text: Which of the following pair of nuclei are isobars of the element?
solution:
Isobars are atoms of different chemical elements that have the same number of nucleons (mass number $A$), but different atomic numbers ($Z$).
In the given options:
(1) $^{3}_{1}\text{H}$ and $^{3}_{2}\text{He}$: Both have the same mass number $A = 3$. Since they have different atomic numbers ($Z = 1$ and $Z = 2$), they are isobars.
(2) $^{2}_{1}\text{H}$ and $^{3}_{1}\text{H}$: These have the same atomic number ($Z = 1$) but different mass numbers. They are isotopes.
(3) $^{198}_{80}\text{Hg}$ and $^{197}_{79}\text{Au}$: These have different mass numbers ($198$ and $197$).
(4) $^{236}_{92}\text{U}$ and $^{238}_{92}\text{U}$: These have the same atomic number ($Z = 92$) but different mass numbers. They are isotopes.
Thus, the pair $^{3}_{1}\text{H}$ and $^{3}_{2}\text{He}$ are isobars.

question_text:
The average energy released per fission for the nucleus of $^{235}_{92}\text{U}$ is $190\text{ MeV}$. When all the atoms of $47\text{ g}$ pure $^{235}_{92}\text{U}$ undergo fission process, the energy released is $\alpha \times 10^{23}\text{ MeV}$. The value of $\alpha$ is $\text{______}$.
$(\text{Avogadro Number} = 6 \times 10^{23}\text{ per mole})$
solution:
The number of $^{235}\text{U}$ atoms in $47\text{ g}$ is determined using Avogadro's number.
Molar mass of $^{235}\text{U}$ is $235\text{ g/mol}$, so the number of moles is $n = 47/235\text{ mol}$.
The total number of atoms is $N = (47/235) \times 6 \times 10^{23}$.
Since each fission releases $190\text{ MeV}$, the total energy released is:
$$E_{\text{total}} = N \times 190 = \frac{47 \times 6 \times 10^{23}}{235} \times 190 = \frac{47 \times 6 \times 190}{235} \times 10^{23}\text{ MeV}.$$
Calculating the numerator: $47 \times 6 \times 190 = 282 \times 190 = 53580$.
Therefore: $E_{\text{total}} = \frac{53580}{235} \times 10^{23} = 228 \times 10^{23}\text{ MeV}$, giving $\alpha = 228$.

Given below are two statements:
Statement I: For all elements, greater the mass of the nucleus, greater is the binding energy per nucleon.
Statement II: For all elements, nuclei with less binding energy per nucleon transforms to nuclei with greater binding energy per nucleon.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.text: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true

solution:
Statement I is false because binding energy per nucleon does not increase monotonically with mass number. It peaks at Iron-56 and decreases for heavier elements.
Statement II is true. It describes the fundamental principle of nuclear reactions: fission of heavy nuclei (low BE/A) and fusion of light nuclei (low BE/A) both produce nuclei with higher binding energy per nucleon, releasing energy in the process. Both processes are energetically favorable for the same reason: moving toward higher stability (higher BE/A).

question_text: A nucleus has mass number $\alpha$ and radius $R_\alpha$. Another nucleus has mass number $\beta$ and radius $R_\beta$. If $\beta = 8\alpha$ then $R_\alpha/R_\beta$ is:
solution:
Nuclear radius follows $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$ where $A$ is mass number.
Given $\beta = 8\alpha$, we have $R_\alpha = R_0 \alpha^{1/3}$ and $R_\beta = R_0 (8\alpha)^{1/3} = R_0 \cdot 2\alpha^{1/3} = 2R_\alpha$.
Thus $R_\alpha/R_\beta = 1/2 = 0.5$.

question_text:
The binding energy per nucleon of $^{209}_{83}Bi$ is $\underline{\hspace{1cm}}$ $\text{MeV}$.

$[\text{Take } m(^{209}_{83}Bi) = 208.980388\text{ u},\ m_p = 1.007825\text{ u},\ m_n = 1.008665\text{ u},\ 1\text{ u} = 931\text{ MeV}/c^2]$
solution:
For the nucleus $^{209}_{83}\text{Bi}$, the number of protons is $Z = 83$ and the number of neutrons is $N = 209 - 83 = 126$.

Mass of 83 protons $= 83 \times 1.007825 = 83.649475\text{ u}$

Mass of 126 neutrons $= 126 \times 1.008665 = 127.091790\text{ u}$

Total mass of the nucleons $= 83.649475 + 127.091790 = 210.741265\text{ u}$

The mass defect $\Delta m$ is given by:

$\Delta m = \text{Total mass of nucleons} - \text{Mass of nucleus}$

$\Delta m = 210.741265 - 208.980388 = 1.760877\text{ u}$

The total binding energy ($BE$) is:

$BE = \Delta m \times 931\text{ MeV}$

$BE = 1.760877 \times 931 = 1639.376\text{ MeV}$

The binding energy per nucleon is:

$\frac{BE}{A} = \frac{1639.376}{209} \approx 7.84\text{ MeV}$

Answer: 7.84

question_text: Two nuclei of mass number $3$ combine with another nucleus of mass number $4$ to yield a nucleus of mass number $10$. If the binding energy per nucleon for the mass numbers $3$, $4$ and $10$ are $5.6\text{ MeV}$, $7.4\text{ MeV}$ and $6.1\text{ MeV}$, respectively, then in the process, $\Delta M c^2 = \underline{\hspace{1cm}}\text{ MeV}$.
solution:
The nuclear reaction is given by:

$2X^3 + Y^4 \to Z^{10}$

The total binding energy of the reactants is the sum of the binding energies of the two nuclei of mass number 3 and the nucleus of mass number 4.

Binding energy of reactants $= 2 \times (3 \times 5.6) + (4 \times 7.4)$

$= 33.6 + 29.6 = 63.2\text{ MeV}$

The total binding energy of the product nucleus of mass number 10 is:

Binding energy of product $= 10 \times 6.1 = 61.0\text{ MeV}$

The change in mass energy $\Delta M c^2$ is equal to the difference in the total binding energies of the reactants and the product.

$\Delta M c^2 = |63.2 - 61.0| = 2.2\text{ MeV}$

Answer: 2.2

question_text:
Assuming the experimental mass of $^{12}_{6}\text{C}$ as $12\text{ u}$, the mass defect of $^{12}_{6}\text{C}$ atom is $\underline{\hspace{1cm}}\text{ MeV}/c^2$.

(Mass of proton $= 1.00727\text{ u}$, mass of neutron $= 1.00866\text{ u}$, $1\text{ u} = 931.5\text{ MeV}/c^2$ and $c$ is the speed of the light in vacuum).
solution:
The mass of 6 protons is $6 \times 1.00727\text{ u} = 6.04362\text{ u}$.

The mass of 6 neutrons is $6 \times 1.00866\text{ u} = 6.05196\text{ u}$.

Total mass of the constituent nucleons is $6.04362\text{ u} + 6.05196\text{ u} = 12.09558\text{ u}$.

The mass defect $\Delta m$ is the difference between the total mass of the nucleons and the experimental mass of the atom (ignoring electron mass as per the given data):

$$\Delta m = 12.09558\text{ u} - 12\text{ u} = 0.09558\text{ u}$$

Converting the mass defect into $\text{MeV}/c^2$:

$$\Delta m = 0.09558 \times 931.5\text{ MeV}/c^2 = 89.03277\text{ MeV}/c^2 \approx 89.03\text{ MeV}/c^2$$

question_text: The energy released when $\frac{7}{17.13}\text{ kg}$ of $^{7}_{3}\text{Li}$ is converted into $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ by proton bombardment is $\alpha \times 10^{32}\text{ eV}$. The value of $\alpha$ is $\underline{\hspace{1cm}}$. (Nearest integer) (Mass of $^{7}_{3}\text{Li} = 7.0183\text{ u}$, mass of $^{4}_{2}\text{He} = 4.004\text{ u}$, mass of proton $= 1.008\text{ u}$ and $1\text{ u} = 931\text{ MeV}/c^2$ and Avogadro number $= 6.0 \times 10^{23}$)
solution:
The nuclear reaction for the proton bombardment of Lithium is:

$$^{7}_{3}\text{Li} + ^{1}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow 2\,^{4}_{2}\text{He}$$

The mass defect ($\Delta m$) for the reaction is:

$$\Delta m = m(^{7}_{3}\text{Li}) + m(^{1}_{1}\text{H}) - 2m(^{4}_{2}\text{He})$$

$$\Delta m = 7.0183 + 1.008 - 2(4.004)$$

$$\Delta m = 8.0263 - 8.008 = 0.0183\text{ u}$$

Energy released per reaction ($Q$) is:

$$Q = \Delta m \times 931\text{ MeV} = 0.0183 \times 931\text{ MeV} = 17.0373\text{ MeV}$$

Number of moles of $^{7}_{3}\text{Li}$ in $\frac{7}{17.13}\text{ kg}$:

$$n = \frac{\frac{7}{17.13} \times 10^3\text{ g}}{7\text{ g/mol}} = \frac{1000}{17.13}\text{ mol}$$

Number of atoms of $^{7}_{3}\text{Li}$:

$$N = n \times N_A = \frac{1000}{17.13} \times 6.0 \times 10^{23} = \frac{6}{17.13} \times 10^{26}$$

Total energy released ($E$) is:

$$E = N \times Q = \left(\frac{6}{17.13} \times 10^{26}\right) \times (17.0373 \times 10^6\text{ eV})$$

$$E = 6 \times \left(\frac{17.0373}{17.13}\right) \times 10^{32}\text{ eV} \approx 6 \times 10^{32}\text{ eV}$$

Therefore, $\alpha = 6$.

question_text: The energy released if hydrogen atoms are combined to form $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ is _______ $\text{MeV}$. (Take binding energies per nucleon of $^{2}_{1}\text{H}$ and $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ as $1.1\text{ MeV}$ and $7.2\text{ MeV}$, respectively)
solution:
The fusion reaction is given by:
$$2^{2}_{1}\text{H} \rightarrow {^{4}_{2}\text{He}}$$

Binding energy of one $^{2}_{1}\text{H}$ nucleus $= 2 \times 1.1 = 2.2\text{ MeV}$
Total initial binding energy $= 2 \times 2.2 = 4.4\text{ MeV}$
Binding energy of $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ nucleus $= 4 \times 7.2 = 28.8\text{ MeV}$

Energy released $\Delta E = \text{Final binding energy} - \text{Initial binding energy}$
$$\Delta E = 28.8 - 4.4 = 24.4\text{ MeV}$$

Answer: $24.4$

question_text: Two radioactive substances A and B of mass numbers $200$ and $212$ respectively, shows spontaneous $\alpha$-decay with same $Q$ value of $1\text{ MeV}$. The ratio of energies of $\alpha$-rays produced by A and B is
solution:
In an $\alpha$-decay, the kinetic energy of the emitted $\alpha$-particle is given by the conservation of momentum and energy as:
$$K_{\alpha} = \frac{A - 4}{A}Q$$
where $A$ is the mass number of the parent nucleus.

For substance A ($A = 200$):
$$K_{\alpha, A} = \frac{200 - 4}{200}Q = \frac{196}{200}Q$$

For substance B ($A = 212$):
$$K_{\alpha, B} = \frac{212 - 4}{212}Q = \frac{208}{212}Q$$

The ratio of the energies of the $\alpha$-rays produced by A and B is:
$$\frac{K_{\alpha, A}}{K_{\alpha, B}} = \frac{\frac{196}{200}Q}{\frac{208}{212}Q} = \frac{196}{200} \times \frac{212}{208}$$

Simplifying the fractions:
$$\frac{K_{\alpha, A}}{K_{\alpha, B}} = \frac{49}{50} \times \frac{53}{52} = \frac{2597}{2600}$$

Answer: $\frac{2597}{2600}$
